item.content:encoded:
Applications are now open for government officials interested in joining the 2026 World Trade Organization Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) Mentoring System as mentees, an international professional development initiative designed to strengthen practical knowledge, peer learning, coordination and engagement on sanitary and phytosanitary issues.

The WTO SPS Mentoring System connects government officials who need support on particular SPS challenges with experienced officials who can provide practical guidance through an informal, flexible mentoring relationship. The initiative is particularly intended to assist developing and least-developed country (LDC) WTO members, including in areas such as SPS transparency, participation in the WTO SPS Committee, implementation of SPS Agreement provisions, domestic coordination, leadership and other operational SPS issues.

Applications for the current call must be submitted by:

Friday, 25 September 2026

The WTO’s current implementation timeline indicates that mentees will be selected during the fourth quarter of 2026, followed by a call for mentors and mentor–mentee matching. The new mentoring relationships are then expected to operate from the first quarter of 2027 onward, with the duration determined by the individual mentoring participants.

The programme is not a scholarship, grant or funded training course. The WTO states that mentoring does not imply a financial commitment unless the participants agree otherwise. Instead, the programme focuses on professional knowledge exchange and practical institutional capacity-building between government officials.

Apply for the 2026 WTO SPS Mentoring System

Official WTO SPS Mentoring System information

About the WTO SPS Mentoring System

The SPS Mentoring System was created by the WTO Committee on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures as a practical mechanism for supporting government officials who work with SPS matters.

It was established following recommendations arising from the Sixth Review of the Operation and Implementation of the SPS Agreement, adopted in March 2025.

The system was originally launched as a pilot in June 2025.

Its purpose was to provide developing and LDC members with additional practical support, particularly concerning:

  • SPS transparency
  • Timely engagement in SPS matters
  • Participation in the SPS Committee
  • Implementation of SPS requirements
  • Domestic institutional coordination
  • Knowledge-sharing between governments

The pilot created mentoring relationships between government officials from different WTO members, including through South-South cooperation.

Following the pilot, the SPS Committee agreed in June 2026 to extend the initiative for another two years, with a mid-term review planned for 2027.

What Are Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures?

Sanitary and phytosanitary measures are government measures intended to protect:

  • Human health
  • Animal health
  • Plant health
  • Food safety

In international trade, these rules can affect products such as:

  • Food
  • Agricultural commodities
  • Plants
  • Animals
  • Meat
  • Fish
  • Fruit and vegetables
  • Seeds
  • Animal products

SPS policy can involve issues including:

  • Food safety standards
  • Pest controls
  • Animal disease measures
  • Plant health regulations
  • Quarantine
  • Import inspections
  • Risk assessment
  • Certification
  • Maximum residue limits
  • Disease-related import restrictions

The WTO SPS Agreement establishes disciplines governing how members use such measures in international trade.

International standards in the SPS field are closely associated with organizations including:

  • The Codex Alimentarius Commission for food safety
  • The World Organisation for Animal Health for animal health and zoonoses
  • The International Plant Protection Convention for plant health

Government officials working in these areas may therefore encounter highly technical questions alongside complex institutional and trade-policy challenges.

The mentoring system is intended to help officials learn from peers who have already dealt with comparable problems.

Why Was the SPS Mentoring System Created?

The WTO SPS Committee recognized that developing and least-developed members may face practical challenges when participating in the SPS system.

These can include:

  • Limited institutional capacity
  • Difficulties coordinating agencies domestically
  • Limited experience preparing SPS notifications
  • Challenges using WTO transparency mechanisms
  • Limited familiarity with SPS Committee procedures
  • Difficulties implementing specific SPS Agreement obligations
  • Technical problems associated with sanitary or phytosanitary controls

The mentoring system offers a relatively flexible mechanism through which government officials can discuss those practical challenges with peers who have relevant experience.

The aim is therefore not simply to provide theoretical training on the SPS Agreement.

It is intended to facilitate problem-oriented learning.

How the Mentoring System Works

The WTO describes mentoring as an:

Informal, ad hoc supportive relationship between government officials.

Its purpose is to facilitate:

  • Knowledge-sharing
  • Peer learning
  • Practical discussion
  • Engagement on SPS-related issues

A mentoring arrangement does not have to consist only of one mentor and one mentee.

Depending on the issue, it may involve:

  • One mentor and one mentee
  • Several mentees
  • Several mentors
  • A wider peer-learning relationship

This flexibility allows the mentoring arrangement to be adapted to the SPS challenge involved.

Mentoring Is Not Formal Consultancy

Participants should not view this programme as equivalent to hiring a technical consultant.

The mentor is primarily a peer professional who can:

  • Share experience
  • Explain approaches used in another administration
  • Discuss institutional practices
  • Suggest useful tools
  • Help the mentee think through practical challenges
  • Share lessons learned

The exact relationship will depend on the needs identified by the mentee and the experience of the mentor.

Possible SPS Mentoring Topics

The WTO identifies several broad areas that may form the basis of a mentoring request.

These include:

SPS Transparency

Transparency is a major component of the WTO SPS system.

Mentoring may help an official understand areas such as:

  • Notifications
  • National enquiry points
  • National notification authorities
  • Information-sharing
  • Changes in SPS regulations
  • Timely communication with trading partners

Officials who are newly responsible for SPS transparency may benefit particularly from practical guidance from another administration.

Participation in the WTO SPS Committee

Another mentoring objective may involve:

SPS Committee participation.

Officials may need support understanding:

  • Committee procedures
  • How to prepare for meetings
  • How to coordinate positions domestically
  • How to raise an SPS issue
  • How to respond to questions
  • How to engage with other WTO members

The mentoring system may therefore support officials who want to strengthen their government’s effective participation in WTO SPS processes.

Operational Implementation of SPS Issues

Officials may also request mentoring concerning the implementation of specific SPS matters.

For example, a government agency could seek peer support concerning:

  • Import inspection
  • Risk categorization
  • Food safety controls
  • Animal health measures
  • Plant health systems
  • Regulatory implementation

The exact issue should be identified in the mentee’s request.

Implementation of the SPS Agreement

Mentoring may concern a particular:

SPS Agreement provision

or a broader implementation problem.

This can be valuable where officials understand the formal legal requirement but need practical examples of how another WTO member has operationalized it.

Leadership and Domestic Coordination

SPS policy frequently involves several government institutions.

Depending on the country, these might include:

  • Ministry of Agriculture
  • Ministry of Health
  • Ministry of Trade
  • Food safety authorities
  • Veterinary authorities
  • Plant protection authorities
  • Customs
  • Standards agencies

Poor coordination can create problems in:

  • Notification
  • International representation
  • Inspection
  • Risk management
  • Trade negotiations
  • Regulatory implementation

The WTO therefore identifies leadership and coordination on SPS matters as a potential mentoring objective.

South-South Cooperation

An important feature of the mentoring system is that it can support:

South-South cooperation.

This means expertise does not need to flow only from high-income countries to developing economies.

Officials in one developing country may have highly relevant experience that can benefit counterparts in another country dealing with a similar institutional or regulatory issue.

For example, the pilot included Morocco providing mentoring on transparency, domestic coordination and SPS Committee participation to officials from Cameroon, Djibouti and Tunisia.

Examples From the First SPS Mentoring Pilot

The 2025–2026 pilot provides useful examples of the kinds of issues that can be addressed.

Belize and the European Union

The Belize Agricultural Health Authority was matched with the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Health and Food Safety.

Their mentoring topic focused on:

SPS risk categorization and/or risk-based inspection.

Cameroon, Djibouti and Tunisia With Morocco

Officials from trade ministries in:

  • Cameroon
  • Djibouti
  • Tunisia

were connected with Morocco’s:

National Office for Food Safety

The mentoring focused on:

  • SPS transparency
  • Domestic coordination
  • SPS Committee participation

Namibia and the United Kingdom

Namibia’s Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform was matched with the UK’s Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs.

The mentoring focus was:

SPS Committee participation.

Pakistan and Canada

Pakistan’s Animal Quarantine Department was connected with the:

Canadian Food Inspection Agency

The mentoring addressed:

  • Operational implementation
  • Domestic coordination

Peru and the European Union

Peru’s National Authority for Health and Safety in Fisheries and Aquaculture was matched with the European Commission.

The mentoring explored:

Artificial intelligence and predictive models based on historical sanitary control data for assessing health risks related to hydrobiological products.

These examples demonstrate the considerable range of issues that may be appropriate for mentoring.

Results of the 2025–2026 Pilot

The initial pilot generated significant interest.

The WTO reported receiving:

56 mentoring requests

from:

23 WTO members and observers.

From those requests:

  • Nine applications were selected
  • Five mentoring partnerships were established

The most common mentoring topics included:

  • Transparency
  • SPS Committee participation
  • Implementation of specific SPS issues or Agreement provisions
  • Leadership
  • Domestic SPS coordination

The positive experience and feedback from participants contributed to the SPS Committee’s decision to continue the programme for another two years.

Who Should Apply in 2026?

The current call is directed at:

Government officials working on SPS matters who want mentoring assistance to address SPS issues at the domestic level.

The programme’s broader purpose is to support:

Developing and least-developed country WTO members.

Potential applicants might therefore work in institutions such as:

  • Ministries of Agriculture
  • Ministries of Trade
  • Ministries of Health
  • Food safety authorities
  • Veterinary services
  • Plant protection agencies
  • Fisheries authorities
  • Quarantine agencies
  • SPS national notification authorities
  • SPS enquiry points
  • Other government regulatory agencies

The key issue is that the applicant should have official responsibilities connected with sanitary or phytosanitary matters.

This Call Is for Mentees

It is important to distinguish between:

Mentees

and:

Mentors

The current application form is specifically for officials requesting mentoring.

The 2026 timeline indicates that:

  1. Mentee applications are collected during Q3 2026.
  2. Mentees are selected during Q4 2026.
  3. A call for mentors follows.
  4. Mentors and mentees are matched.
  5. Mentoring begins afterward.

Government officials who are interested in providing mentoring rather than receiving it should therefore follow the subsequent mentor call rather than complete the mentee form.

What Makes a Strong Mentee Request?

The first pilot indicates that selection can consider factors such as:

  • The mentoring objective
  • Commitment of the mentee
  • Language
  • Region
  • The suitability of available mentors

A strong application should therefore identify a specific SPS challenge rather than requesting general professional development.

For example, compare these two requests:

“Help me learn more about SPS.”

versus:

“Our agency wants to strengthen its coordination between the national notification authority and veterinary and plant health regulators so that SPS notifications are submitted more consistently and on time.”

The second request provides a much clearer basis for identifying a suitable mentor.

What Applicants Should Explain

Although applicants should follow the actual online application questions, a useful mentoring request will normally make clear:

  • What SPS issue the official is working on
  • What specific problem they are trying to solve
  • Why mentoring would be useful
  • What outcome they hope to achieve
  • What their role is within the responsible government institution
  • How they intend to participate actively
  • Any relevant language or regional considerations

The programme is based on active peer learning, so mentees should be prepared to engage consistently rather than simply receive information.

There Is No Financial Award

Applicants should understand that the WTO SPS Mentoring System is:

Not a financial assistance programme.

The WTO states that:

Mentoring does not imply any financial commitment unless otherwise agreed.

Therefore, applicants should not expect:

  • A stipend
  • Salary
  • Scholarship
  • Research grant
  • Travel allowance
  • Cash award

The value of the programme lies primarily in:

  • Professional mentoring
  • Knowledge exchange
  • Peer learning
  • Institutional capacity-building
  • International SPS networking

Mentoring Duration

The programme does not prescribe one universal duration for every mentoring relationship.

According to the current implementation timeline:

The duration will be decided by each mentoring pair.

The new 2026 cohort is expected to begin mentoring from:

Q1 2027 onward.

This flexibility allows different SPS problems to receive different levels of support.

Current 2026–2028 Timeline

The WTO’s current schedule provides a useful overview.

Period Activity
March 2025 SPS Committee recommends exploring a mentoring system
June 2026 Committee agrees to extend the programme
Q3 2026 Call for mentees
25 September 2026 Mentee application deadline
Q4 2026 Selection of mentees
Q4 2026 Call for mentors and matching
Q1 2027 onward Mentoring begins
March 2027 Intermediate reporting
June 2027 Intermediate reporting and mid-term review
Q3 2027 New call for mentees
Q4 2027 Further matching
2028 Continued mentoring and Committee reporting
November 2028 Committee considers whether to extend the initiative again

Why the WTO Extended the Programme

The pilot generated positive feedback from WTO members involved in the mentoring partnerships.

At the June 2026 SPS Committee meeting, several participating members shared their experiences, and the Committee agreed to extend the programme for two additional years.

The extension suggests that WTO members see peer mentoring as a useful complement to more conventional forms of:

  • Technical assistance
  • Training
  • Workshops
  • Capacity-building

Mentoring allows officials to engage with a colleague over time rather than receiving information only during a short formal training event.

Why SPS Capacity Matters for International Trade

SPS measures play an important role in determining whether agricultural and food products can enter international markets.

Weak SPS capacity can affect a country’s ability to:

  • Export agricultural products
  • Respond to trading partner requirements
  • Demonstrate food safety
  • Control pests and animal diseases
  • Participate effectively in international rule-making
  • Respond to SPS trade concerns

At the same time, governments need to protect:

  • Consumers
  • Agricultural production
  • Animal health
  • Plant health

Officials therefore often need to balance:

Trade facilitation and market access

with:

Legitimate health protection.

The mentoring programme can help officials learn how other administrations address this balance.

Transparency as a Major Priority

Transparency has been one of the recurring priorities of the SPS Committee.

WTO members are expected to communicate relevant SPS measures and provide mechanisms through which trading partners can obtain information.

For developing and LDC members, effective transparency may require:

  • Strong domestic coordination
  • Clear institutional responsibility
  • Trained staff
  • Reliable information flows
  • Familiarity with WTO systems

This explains why transparency has featured prominently in both the programme’s objectives and its pilot mentoring relationships.

Connection With SPS Committee Participation

The SPS Committee provides a regular forum in which WTO members discuss:

  • Implementation of the SPS Agreement
  • Specific trade concerns
  • Transparency
  • International standards
  • Technical cooperation
  • Emerging SPS issues

Officials who understand how to participate effectively can better represent their government’s interests.

The mentoring system can therefore support institutional capacity not only at the domestic level but also in multilateral trade diplomacy.

Application Deadline

The deadline for the current mentee call is:

Friday, 25 September 2026.

The WTO’s official current timeline explicitly lists this date for the Q3 2026 mentee call.

Applicants should submit early rather than waiting until the final day.

How to Apply

Government officials interested in receiving SPS mentoring should complete the official:

2026 SPS Mentoring System – Form to Request Mentoring for Mentees

Complete the WTO SPS Mentoring application form

Applicants should also review the programme information before submitting.

Read the official WTO SPS Mentoring System information

Tips for Preparing a Strong Application

1. Identify One Concrete SPS Problem

Avoid requesting mentoring on “SPS generally.”

Instead, identify a specific problem such as:

  • Improving SPS notification procedures
  • Strengthening domestic coordination
  • Improving risk-based inspections
  • Preparing for SPS Committee participation
  • Implementing a specific Agreement obligation

Specificity makes it easier for the WTO to identify a relevant mentor.

2. Explain the Institutional Context

Explain what your agency does and what role you personally play.

For example:

  • Are you responsible for notifications?
  • Do you work on veterinary import controls?
  • Do you coordinate plant health regulation?
  • Do you represent your government in WTO meetings?

This context helps demonstrate why the mentoring request is relevant.

3. Define a Practical Objective

A good mentoring objective should be achievable.

For example:

“Develop a more effective national SPS coordination procedure involving the trade, agriculture and health ministries.”

is stronger than:

“Improve SPS capacity.”

4. Show Willingness to Participate Actively

The pilot considered mentee commitment as part of the selection process.

Mentoring works only when both sides actively participate.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to:

  • Attend agreed meetings
  • Share relevant information
  • Follow up on discussions
  • Test proposed approaches
  • Report progress

5. Think About Language

Language is one factor considered when matching mentors and mentees.

Applicants should accurately indicate which languages they can use professionally.

This increases the likelihood of an effective mentoring relationship.

6. Explain the Wider Institutional Benefit

Where possible, show how mentoring could benefit more than one person.

For example:

  • Improved procedures
  • Better coordination
  • Knowledge transferred to colleagues
  • More effective WTO participation
  • Stronger national transparency

This can make the request more strategically valuable.

Key Details at a Glance

Programme: WTO SPS Mentoring System

Organization: World Trade Organization

Responsible body: WTO Committee on Sanitary and Phytosanitary Measures

Current call: 2026 call for mentees

Target participants: Government officials working on SPS matters

Primary intended beneficiaries: Developing and least-developed country WTO members

Format: Flexible professional mentoring

Relationship: Informal, ad hoc and peer-based

Potential format: One-to-one or multi-person mentoring

Areas: Transparency, Committee participation, implementation, leadership, coordination and other SPS issues

Financial support: None automatically provided

Mentee application deadline: 25 September 2026

Selection: Q4 2026

Mentor recruitment and matching: Q4 2026

Mentoring start: Q1 2027 onward

Duration: Determined by each mentoring pair

Mid-term review: June 2027

Conclusion

The WTO SPS Mentoring System 2026 provides government officials working on sanitary and phytosanitary matters with an opportunity to receive practical, peer-based professional support on specific SPS challenges.

Established following the Sixth Review of the SPS Agreement and first piloted in 2025–2026, the system was created to assist developing and least-developed WTO members, particularly in strengthening transparency and timely engagement on SPS matters.

The programme is deliberately flexible. Mentoring can involve one mentor and one mentee or several participants and can address issues ranging from SPS transparency and WTO Committee participation to domestic coordination, risk-based inspection and practical implementation of SPS obligations.

The first pilot received 56 requests from 23 members and observers, resulting in nine selected applications and five mentoring partnerships. Following positive feedback from participating members, the SPS Committee agreed in June 2026 to extend the system for a further two years.

This is not a financial award. Mentees should not expect a stipend, salary or travel grant. Rather, the value lies in access to peer experience, professional knowledge, practical problem-solving and stronger engagement with the international SPS community.

For government officials in developing and least-developed countries who are currently dealing with a specific sanitary or phytosanitary challenge, the programme can provide a relatively personalized form of capacity-building that complements formal WTO technical assistance.

Applications for the current mentee cohort must be submitted by:

25 September 2026.

The appointment may be renewed for up to two years, depending on performance and availability of funding.

About CIDER

The Cornell Collaboration for International Development Economics Research (CIDER) is a cross-campus initiative involving faculty from several Cornell University units, including the SC Johnson College of Business, College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, College of Arts and Sciences, and the Cornell Jeb E. Brooks School of Public Policy.

CIDER brings together faculty working across international development economics and related areas, including poverty, food insecurity, agricultural and rural development, labor markets, nutrition, resilience and structural transformation.

The initiative emphasizes rigorous applied research designed to generate evidence that can inform public and private decision-makers around the world.

Key Responsibilities

Successful candidates will contribute to a variety of research and academic activities.

Research Support

Responsibilities include:

  • Supporting faculty Principal Investigators and research teams in planning, designing and implementing research projects.
  • Assisting with research activities and data collection.
  • Collecting, cleaning, managing and analyzing secondary data.
  • Developing and maintaining research code used to organize and analyze data.
  • Supporting the design, implementation, monitoring and updating of research surveys.
  • Working with partner organizations involved in research implementation and data collection.
  • Conducting literature reviews and synthesizing research findings.
  • Assisting with manuscripts, conference presentations and research talks.
  • Supporting grant and funding reports, Institutional Review Board submissions and other research documentation.

Administrative Support

Fellows may also:

  • Prepare materials and resources for CIDER programmes, events and initiatives.
  • Provide logistical and administrative support for virtual and in-person training programmes, workshops and seminars.

Professional Development

The position also provides opportunities for fellows to:

  • Participate in research seminar series.
  • Engage in Cornell University’s broader intellectual community.
  • Participate in professional development and training opportunities.
  • Access research-related training through CIDER and other Cornell units.
  • Potentially serve as a teaching assistant for a related course by mutual agreement with supervising faculty.

Salary and Benefits

The Cornell CIDER Pre-Doctoral Research Fellowship is a paid full-time position.

The stated salary range is:

$65,447 – $75,632 per year

The actual hiring rate may depend on factors including prior relevant experience, education, applicable skills and academic discipline.

Cornell also lists a range of employee benefits, including:

  • Health care options
  • Retirement contributions
  • Wellness programmes
  • Employee discounts
  • Vacation and personal leave
  • Paid holidays
  • Winter break
  • Educational benefits
  • Tuition-related programmes
  • Professional development opportunities

Eligibility Requirements

Candidates should have a Bachelor’s degree in economics, business, public policy, mathematics, statistics or a related field, together with 2 to 4 years of relevant experience or an equivalent combination of education and experience.

Applicants should also have:

  • Previous coursework in econometrics and statistics.
  • Familiarity with statistical software such as Stata or R.
  • Strong knowledge of economics research techniques and/or methods.
  • Strong analytical and problem-solving skills.
  • Strong organizational skills and attention to detail.
  • Ability to manage multiple projects.
  • Excellent professional verbal, written and presentation skills.
  • Ability to work independently and collaboratively.
  • Ability to meet deadlines.
  • Ability to seek, coordinate and appropriately disseminate information.
  • Experience working directly with people from different socioeconomic backgrounds.
  • Experience incorporating perspectives from multiple communities.

Preferred Qualifications

The following qualifications are preferred but are not mandatory:

  • A Master’s degree in economics, business, public policy, mathematics, statistics or a related field.
  • Relevant research experience, such as a senior thesis.
  • Experience with additional data analysis, programming or GIS tools.
  • Knowledge of tools such as ArcGIS, Python or SQL.
  • Foreign-language proficiency, particularly in French, Spanish, Swahili, Tamil and/or Portuguese.

Visa and Work Location

The position is onsite at Cornell University’s Ithaca Main Campus in New York.

The posting states that individuals with F-1 OPT/STEM OPT can apply. It also states that no other visa sponsorship or relocation assistance is available for this position.

Who Should Apply?

This opportunity is particularly relevant to graduates who:

  • Have completed a Bachelor’s degree in a relevant discipline.
  • Want to pursue doctoral studies.
  • Are interested in development economics or related research fields.
  • Have quantitative research and data-analysis skills.
  • Have coursework or experience in econometrics and statistics.
  • Want to gain experience working with university researchers.
  • Are interested in academic research and potentially pursuing a PhD.
  • Have an interest in international development research.

Applicants should demonstrate their research interests, relevant quantitative research experience and skills, as well as their interest in pursuing doctoral study.

How to Apply

Applicants are required to submit a resume and cover letter explaining their research interests, relevant quantitative research experience and skills, and their interest in pursuing doctoral study.

Cornell indicates that most positions require applicants to apply online and submit both a resume/CV and cover letter.

Application Deadline

15 October 2026

Applications received by October 15, 2026, will receive full consideration. Applications submitted after this date may still be considered until the positions are filled.

Apply

Interested candidates should apply through the official Cornell University careers platform and follow the online submission instructions provided in the job posting.

Contact Information

Contact Name: Melissa Dorward-Bauman

Contact Email: msm298@cornell.edu

Why Consider This Opportunity?

The Cornell CIDER Pre-Doctoral Research Fellowship offers an opportunity for aspiring doctoral researchers to gain substantial practical experience before entering a PhD programme.

Participants can work alongside faculty researchers, contribute to development economics research, strengthen their quantitative research abilities and participate in seminars and professional development activities.

For graduates considering doctoral study in economics, development studies, public policy or related disciplines, the position can provide valuable exposure to the academic research environment and help strengthen their preparation for future PhD applications.

Conclusion

The Cornell CIDER Pre-Doctoral Research Fellowship 2026 is an excellent opportunity for qualified graduates seeking to build strong research experience before pursuing doctoral studies.

The full-time position combines hands-on research, quantitative data analysis, academic engagement and professional development at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York. Successful candidates will work with faculty on development economics research while gaining exposure to the wider intellectual life of one of the world’s leading research universities.

Qualified applicants should prepare a strong resume and cover letter highlighting their research experience, quantitative skills and doctoral ambitions, and submit their applications before the 15 October 2026 full-consideration deadline.

Discover more fellowship opportunities on the OFY Webpage.

item.content:encoded:
The Siemens Energy Education and Development (SEED) Solar PV Installation (SPVI) Training is offering professionals and technicians an opportunity to strengthen their technical knowledge and practical skills in solar photovoltaic installation and renewable energy technologies. The training is supported by the Nigerian Energy Support Programme (NESP), a technical assistance programme co-funded by the European Union and the German Government and implemented by GIZ.

Designed to respond to the growing demand for technically competent renewable energy professionals, the programme combines classroom-based theoretical instruction with practical, hands-on learning, technical site visits and competency assessments. Successful participants will also receive COREN Certification upon completion of the training.

Importantly, the training itself is offered free of charge, and the cost of certification is also covered. Meals will be provided on training days, although participants will be responsible for their own accommodation and transportation.

The particular training stream covered by the application form will be conducted in Lagos State and Abeokuta, Ogun State, with participants required to attend the training in person for three weeks in September 2026.

About the SEED Solar PV Installation Training

The SEED Solar PV Installation Training is focused on developing practical and technical capacity in the renewable energy sector, particularly for individuals who are working or intending to work in solar photovoltaic installation and related areas.

Solar photovoltaic technology is increasingly important in the transition towards cleaner and more accessible energy. As demand for solar energy systems continues to grow, there is a corresponding need for technicians and professionals who possess the technical competencies required to install, operate and work with solar PV systems safely and effectively.

The training therefore provides an opportunity for participants to develop competencies that can support their professional development and participation in Nigeria’s renewable energy industry.

Rather than being limited exclusively to applicants with conventional academic qualifications, the programme specifically encourages applications from individuals coming through both formal educational pathways and practical or experience-based pathways.

This makes the opportunity particularly relevant to people who have gained technical knowledge through education as well as those whose skills have been developed through hands-on work and practical experience.

Who Is Organising and Supporting the Training?

The training is associated with the Siemens Energy Education and Development (SEED) initiative and is supported by the Nigerian Energy Support Programme (NESP).

NESP is described in the application information as a technical assistance programme that is:

  • Co-funded by the European Union.
  • Co-funded by the German Government.
  • Implemented by GIZ.

Through this support, the programme is designed to contribute to technical capacity development in Nigeria’s renewable energy sector.

The involvement of these institutions also makes the training relevant to broader efforts to improve technical skills and strengthen the renewable energy workforce.

What Does the Solar PV Installation Training Cover?

The programme is structured around several complementary forms of learning. Participants will not only receive theoretical information but will also have opportunities to apply their knowledge in practical settings.

The training will combine:

1. Theoretical Instruction

Participants will receive theoretical instruction designed to build their understanding of solar PV installation and related technical concepts.

The theoretical component provides an important foundation for practical work because solar PV installation requires technicians to understand how systems function, how different components interact and how installations should be approached from a technical and safety perspective.

2. Hands-On Practical Training

A major component of the programme is practical training.

Participants will have the opportunity to develop their technical competencies through hands-on activities rather than relying solely on classroom instruction. This practical focus can be particularly valuable for people preparing to enter the renewable energy sector or professionals seeking to strengthen existing technical skills.

3. Technical Site Visits

The programme will also include technical site visits.

Site visits can provide participants with exposure to practical applications of renewable energy technologies and help connect theoretical concepts with real-world installations and working environments.

This component is particularly useful for participants who want to understand how solar PV systems and technical processes are applied beyond a classroom setting.

4. Competency Assessments

The training will include competency assessments to evaluate participants’ knowledge and practical capabilities.

Assessment is an important part of technical training because it provides an opportunity to demonstrate that the competencies developed during the programme can be applied effectively.

5. COREN Certification

Participants who successfully complete the training will receive COREN Certification, according to the application information.

The certification component adds an important professional dimension to the programme and may be valuable to individuals seeking to strengthen their professional credentials in the technical and engineering-related space.

Training Locations

For this particular stream, training will take place at two locations:

  • Lagos State
  • Abeokuta, Ogun State

Applicants are required to indicate their preferred training location when completing the application form.

The form provides the following location choices:

  1. Abeokuta, Ogun State
  2. Lagos State

Applicants should therefore consider their ability to attend their selected location before submitting the application.

Three-Week In-Person Training Requirement

One of the most important requirements stated in the application form is the ability to attend the programme in person for three weeks during September 2026.

The application specifically asks candidates whether they are able to attend the training physically for three weeks.

This means that the opportunity is not presented as an online training programme. Applicants should be prepared to participate physically at one of the designated training locations.

Before applying, prospective participants should therefore consider:

  • Their availability throughout the three-week training period.
  • Their ability to travel to and from the selected training location.
  • Their ability to arrange accommodation if they live outside the training location.
  • Their ability to cover transportation costs.
  • Their ability to attend the required training activities in person.

Is the SEED Solar PV Installation Training Free?

Yes. The training is stated to be free of charge.

The programme information specifically indicates that:

  • The training is free.
  • The cost of certification is free.
  • Meals will be provided on training days.

This significantly reduces the direct cost of participating in the programme and makes the opportunity accessible to individuals who may otherwise find professional technical training financially difficult to pursue.

However, applicants should carefully note that not every participation-related expense is covered.

What Costs Are Not Covered?

While the training and certification are free, GIZ-NESP and Siemens Energy will not provide accommodation or transportation support during the training.

Participants should therefore make their own arrangements for these costs.

This means that applicants travelling from another city or location may need to budget for:

  • Transportation to and from the training location.
  • Local transportation where necessary.
  • Accommodation for the duration of the training, if required.
  • Any other personal expenses not specifically identified as covered by the programme.

The provision of meals on training days can help reduce daily expenses, but participants should still make adequate arrangements for other costs associated with attending a three-week in-person programme.

Who Is Encouraged to Apply?

The training is designed primarily for individuals interested in developing or strengthening their technical and practical competencies in the renewable energy sector.

The application information specifically describes the target audience as:

  • Professionals working in the renewable energy sector.
  • Technicians working in the renewable energy sector.
  • Professionals seeking to work in the renewable energy sector.
  • Technicians seeking to work in the renewable energy sector.
  • Individuals coming through formal educational backgrounds.
  • Individuals coming through practical or experience-based pathways.

The inclusion of both formal and experience-based pathways is an important feature of the programme.

Applicants should therefore not assume that only people with traditional academic qualifications can apply. The information explicitly encourages candidates with practical or experience-based backgrounds to submit applications.

Formal and Experience-Based Applicants

One of the notable aspects of this opportunity is its recognition of different routes through which people develop technical competencies.

Applicants with Formal Education

Individuals who have acquired relevant knowledge through formal education may find the programme useful for strengthening their technical and practical capabilities.

Academic or technical education can provide theoretical foundations, while practical training can help participants apply that knowledge in real-world settings.

Applicants with Practical Experience

The programme also welcomes applicants who have developed their knowledge and abilities through practical experience.

This is significant for technicians and other individuals who may have gained skills through hands-on work rather than exclusively through formal academic programmes.

The application information therefore takes a broader approach to technical capacity development by recognising both educational and practical pathways.

What Are the Requirements for Applicants?

Based on the information provided in the application form, prospective participants should meet the following key conditions:

  • Have an interest in working in the renewable energy sector, or already be working in the sector.
  • Be a professional or technician seeking to develop relevant competencies.
  • Be willing to participate in the technical and practical components of the programme.
  • Be able to attend the training in person for three weeks in September 2026.
  • Select either Lagos State or Abeokuta, Ogun State as the preferred training location.
  • Be prepared to arrange their own accommodation and transportation.
  • Be able to commit to the programme’s training requirements.

The application form also requests basic personal and contact information, including the applicant’s full name, gender, phone number and email address.

Information Required on the Application Form

Applicants should be prepared to provide several details when completing the application.

The form requests:

  1. Full Name
    Applicants are asked to provide their surname and first name.
  2. Gender
    The available options shown in the form are:

    • Female
    • Male
  3. Phone Number
    Applicants must provide a telephone contact.
  4. Email Address
    A valid email address is required for the application.
  5. Preferred Training Location
    Applicants can select:

    • Abeokuta, Ogun State
    • Lagos State
  6. Availability for In-Person Training
    Applicants must confirm whether they can attend the training in person for three weeks from September 2026.

The form identifies the questions as required, meaning applicants should ensure that the requested information is completed before submitting the application.

Important Google Account and Privacy Notice

The application is presented through Google Forms. The form indicates that the name, email address and photo associated with the applicant’s Google Account will be recorded when the applicant uploads files and submits the form.

Applicants should therefore review the information associated with the Google Account they use when accessing the application and ensure that they are comfortable with the information being recorded as part of the submission process.

Why This Training Opportunity Is Valuable

The SEED Solar PV Installation Training provides several potential benefits for people interested in renewable energy and technical careers.

Free Technical Training

The programme removes the tuition cost associated with the training. Participants do not have to pay for the training itself.

Free Certification

The cost of certification is also covered, meaning participants can complete the programme without paying the stated certification costs.

Practical Skills Development

The hands-on nature of the training can help participants develop practical competencies relevant to solar PV installation.

Exposure to Real-World Applications

Technical site visits can provide participants with exposure to practical applications and professional environments within the renewable energy field.

Competency Assessment

Participants will have their competencies assessed as part of the training, providing a structured way of evaluating the knowledge and skills developed during the programme.

COREN Certification

Successful completion comes with COREN Certification, according to the information provided in the application form.

Meals During Training Days

Meals will be provided on training days, helping to reduce some of the daily expenses associated with attending the programme.

Opportunity for Different Educational Backgrounds

The programme encourages applications from both formally educated candidates and individuals whose competencies have been developed through practical experience.

Things Applicants Should Consider Before Applying

Although the training is free, prospective applicants should carefully consider the logistical requirements.

The programme is in person, and participants must attend for three weeks. This makes availability one of the most important considerations before submitting an application.

Applicants should also remember that accommodation and transportation are not provided.

Someone living outside Lagos or Abeokuta, for example, should determine whether they can realistically travel to the training location and remain there for the duration of the programme.

A strong applicant should therefore:

  • Confirm availability for the full three-week period.
  • Select a training location they can reasonably access.
  • Plan transportation in advance.
  • Arrange accommodation independently if necessary.
  • Ensure their phone number and email address are accurate.
  • Review all required application questions before submission.
  • Use an appropriate Google Account when completing the form.
  • Submit the application with accurate personal information.

Deadline for the SEED Solar PV Installation Training Application

Deadline: Not specified in the application information provided.

The supplied application form states that the training will take place for three weeks from September 2026, but it does not provide a specific application closing date.

Applicants should therefore verify the application page for any updated closing date or submission instructions before applying. Since the training is scheduled for September 2026, prospective applicants should avoid waiting until the last moment to complete the form.

APPLY HERE

How to Apply for the SEED Solar PV Installation Training

Interested applicants should complete the official SEED Solar PV Installation Training application form and provide the required personal and contact information.

The application requires candidates to select their preferred location between Abeokuta, Ogun State and Lagos State and confirm that they can attend the training physically for three weeks in September 2026.

Applicants should ensure that all required sections are completed accurately before submitting the form.

Visit HERE to learn more about the SEED Solar PV Installation Training 2026.

Conclusion

The SEED Solar PV Installation Training presents an important opportunity for professionals and technicians who want to strengthen their technical competencies and pursue opportunities in Nigeria’s growing renewable energy sector. Supported through the Nigerian Energy Support Programme and implemented by GIZ, with Siemens Energy involved through the SEED initiative, the programme combines theoretical learning, hands-on practical training, technical site visits and competency assessments.

One of the strongest features of the opportunity is that the training and certification are free, while meals are provided on training days. Participants should, however, be prepared to cover their own accommodation and transportation expenses.

The programme is also notable for welcoming candidates from both formal educational and practical, experience-based backgrounds. This broad approach gives technicians and aspiring renewable energy professionals with different educational pathways an opportunity to develop relevant skills.

Applicants should pay particular attention to the three-week, in-person attendance requirement in Lagos or Abeokuta, Ogun State, and should confirm that they can commit to the programme before applying. Since no specific application deadline is provided in the supplied information, prospective applicants should check the official application form for the latest submission information.

For more global training opportunities visit OFY HERE.

item.content:encoded:
The Government of Japan is inviting applications from young South Africans interested in gaining international teaching and cultural exchange experience through the Japan Exchange and Teaching (JET) Programme 2027. The programme offers successful participants an opportunity to spend at least one year in Japan working as Assistant Language Teachers (ALTs) while contributing to internationalisation, foreign-language education, and people-to-people exchange at the local level.

Administered through a collaboration involving Japanese government ministries and agencies, the JET Programme is one of the world’s largest international exchange programmes. It brings university graduates from participating countries to Japan to work with local governments, schools, boards of education, and other organisations.

For South African graduates with an interest in education, language, Japanese culture, international relations, community engagement, and cross-cultural communication, the JET Programme provides an opportunity to live and work in Japan while developing professional and intercultural skills.

JET Programme 2027 Overview

The Japan Exchange and Teaching (JET) Programme was established to promote grassroots internationalisation in Japan. Participants work with local communities and educational institutions, helping strengthen understanding between Japan and other countries.

For the 2027 intake, the Embassy of Japan in South Africa is calling for applications from young South Africans who would like to spend at least one year in Japan as Assistant Language Teachers.

Key details

  • Programme: Japan Exchange and Teaching (JET) Programme
  • 2027 Position: Assistant Language Teacher (ALT)
  • Host country: Japan
  • Recruiting country: South Africa
  • Duration: Generally one year
  • Target applicants: Young South African university graduates
  • Work environment: Elementary, junior high and senior high schools, local boards of education and related institutions
  • Application method: Courier with a tracking number or hand delivery
  • Application deadline: 4:00 PM, 16 October 2026
  • Application location: Embassy of Japan, 259 Baines Street, Groenkloof, Pretoria, 0181
  • Selection notification: Successful and unsuccessful applicants will be contacted by email

What Is the JET Programme?

The JET Programme is an international exchange initiative administered through cooperation among several Japanese institutions, including the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC), Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA), Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT), and the Council of Local Authorities for International Relations (CLAIR).

Its primary objective is to promote grassroots internationalisation at the local level.

Rather than focusing only on international exchange at the national or diplomatic level, the programme places participants directly within Japanese communities. Participants interact with students, teachers, local government employees and community members, allowing cultural exchange to take place through everyday professional and community activities.

The programme also seeks to create long-term international networks. Participants are expected to contribute positively to mutual understanding between Japan and their home countries while gaining a deeper understanding of Japanese society and culture.

JET Programme History and Global Reach

The JET Programme has developed considerably since its establishment in 1987.

According to the Embassy of Japan in South Africa, the programme began with participants from only four countries. Over the years, it has expanded to include participants from 54 countries, with 5,993 participants as of 2025.

Across the history of the programme, more than 80,000 people from 82 countries have participated.

This extensive international participation demonstrates the scale of the JET Programme and its emphasis on creating connections between Japan and communities around the world.

The programme has also developed a strong reputation both within Japan and internationally. Participants are regarded as representatives of their respective countries and are therefore expected to conduct themselves responsibly and contribute constructively to international understanding.

Assistant Language Teacher Position

The 2027 opportunity highlighted by the Embassy of Japan in South Africa is for applicants interested in serving as Assistant Language Teachers (ALTs).

ALTs are primarily placed in educational settings, including:

  • Local boards of education
  • Elementary schools
  • Junior high schools
  • Senior high schools

Participants work under the guidance of language-teacher consultants, Japanese teachers of foreign languages, school principals, boards of education, or other designated supervisors.

The precise working environment and responsibilities can vary depending on the Contracting Organisation to which an individual is assigned.

Duties and Responsibilities of an ALT

The role is broader than simply standing in front of a classroom and teaching English. Participants can become involved in different educational and cultural activities depending on the needs of their school or Contracting Organisation.

Typical responsibilities may include the following.

1. Assisting with foreign-language classes

ALTs assist Japanese teachers with foreign-language lessons in elementary, junior high and senior high schools.

This can involve supporting classroom activities, language practice, communication exercises and other activities designed to help students develop their foreign-language abilities.

The exact nature of classroom involvement may depend on the school, teaching arrangements and instructions provided by the relevant supervisor.

2. Supporting foreign-language activities in elementary schools

Participants may also assist with foreign-language activities for younger learners.

This gives ALTs an opportunity to introduce language learning in engaging and accessible ways while interacting directly with Japanese pupils.

3. Helping prepare teaching materials

ALTs may contribute to the preparation of materials used for foreign-language education.

This could involve helping teachers develop language-learning resources or providing information and examples that support classroom instruction.

4. Supporting language training for teachers

Participants may assist with language training for Japanese teachers of foreign languages or other language-related activities.

Their perspective as international participants can be useful in providing practical language knowledge and insights into how English and other foreign languages are used.

5. Participating in extracurricular and club activities

The JET Programme can extend beyond formal classroom instruction.

ALTs may cooperate with extracurricular activities and school clubs, allowing them to interact with students in less formal educational environments.

6. Providing language-related information

Participants may provide information to teachers and language consultants on matters such as:

  • Word usage
  • Pronunciation
  • Language expressions
  • Other language-related subjects

This responsibility allows participants to contribute their knowledge of their own language and culture to the Japanese education system.

7. Supporting foreign-language speech contests

ALTs may also assist with foreign-language speech contests.

This could include helping students prepare, providing language-related guidance or supporting the organisation of such activities, depending on the requirements of the school or Contracting Organisation.

8. Supporting local international exchange activities

One of the most important elements of the JET Programme is international exchange.

Participants may cooperate in local international exchange activities, helping communities develop greater awareness and understanding of other countries and cultures.

9. Performing other duties as required

Participants may be assigned additional duties considered necessary by their supervisor or school principal.

Because assignments differ between Contracting Organisations, applicants should understand that the precise responsibilities of an ALT can vary.

Where Do JET Participants Work?

JET participants are generally appointed by Japanese prefectures, municipalities, private schools and other Contracting Organisations.

This means that successful applicants are not necessarily assigned to one specific city or region in Japan. Their eventual placement depends on the organisation to which they are appointed.

Participants can therefore expect their experience to be shaped partly by their assigned community, school and local working environment.

For someone interested in experiencing Japanese life beyond major tourist destinations, this aspect of the programme can be particularly significant because placements can connect participants with local communities and educational institutions.

One-Year Participation Period

Participants are generally appointed for a one-year period.

The programme is therefore designed as a substantial international experience rather than a short-term visit. Successful applicants should be prepared to live and work in Japan for the duration of their appointment.

The Embassy of Japan also emphasises that participants should avoid withdrawing from the programme after receiving an assignment or ending their participation early, as doing so can create significant difficulties for the Contracting Organisation and affect the administration of the programme.

Applicants should therefore consider the commitment carefully before applying.

Financial Support and Transportation

According to the Embassy of Japan’s information, the cost of transportation from the participant’s place of origin to Japan, as well as remuneration, is funded by Japanese taxpayers through the Contracting Organisation where the participant is appointed.

This means successful participants receive financial support connected to their participation and employment under the programme.

Because participants serve as staff members of their respective Contracting Organisations, they are expected to observe applicable rules and behave responsibly.

The financial arrangements therefore form part of a broader employment and public-service structure rather than being simply a study-abroad scholarship.

Professional and Personal Development Opportunities

The JET Programme can provide participants with an opportunity to develop skills that extend beyond language education.

Living and working in another country can expose participants to new professional environments, educational systems and cultural practices.

Participants can potentially develop experience in areas such as:

  • Classroom support and education
  • Public speaking and communication
  • Cross-cultural communication
  • Community engagement
  • International relations
  • Cultural exchange
  • Teamwork
  • Adaptability
  • Interpersonal communication
  • Working in a foreign professional environment
  • Understanding Japanese society and culture

For graduates interested in careers involving international development, education, communications, diplomacy, international organisations, cultural exchange or global affairs, such experience can provide useful exposure.

Expectations of JET Participants

JET participants are regarded as representatives of their respective countries.

The Embassy of Japan therefore stresses the importance of responsible behaviour and mutual understanding.

Applicants should understand that the programme is not solely about travelling to Japan. Participants are expected to make a meaningful contribution to the communities in which they live and work.

The Embassy indicates that desirable participants should be:

  • Adaptable
  • Mentally capable of performing their duties
  • Physically capable of performing their duties
  • Deeply interested in Japan
  • Responsible in their activities
  • Committed to promoting mutual understanding between nations

Participants should therefore be prepared to adapt to a different cultural and professional environment.

Why the International Exchange Element Matters

International exchange is central to the JET Programme.

An ALT from South Africa, for example, does more than assist with language education. Their presence can give Japanese students and community members opportunities to learn about South Africa and interact with someone from a different cultural background.

At the same time, the participant gains first-hand exposure to Japanese culture and society.

This two-way exchange is one of the fundamental purposes of the programme.

Participants are encouraged to build relationships with the communities where they are placed, contributing to a broader international network that can continue beyond their period in Japan.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The opportunity is particularly relevant to young South African university graduates who are interested in combining professional experience with international cultural exchange.

Potentially suitable applicants may include graduates interested in:

  • Teaching and education
  • English-language education
  • International exchange
  • Japanese culture
  • International development
  • Global communication
  • Community engagement
  • Cross-cultural relations
  • International careers

Applicants should also be comfortable with the responsibilities associated with representing their country in an international programme.

Application Deadline for JET Programme 2027

The deadline is 4:00 PM on 16 October 2026.

Importantly, applications must arrive at the Embassy of Japan by the deadline. Applicants should therefore not wait until the final day to send their documents.

The Embassy specifically instructs applicants to either courier their complete application package with a tracking number or hand deliver it to the designated address.

Application address

Embassy of Japan
JET Programme
259 Baines Street
Groenkloof
Pretoria
0181
South Africa

Applicants using courier services should allow sufficient time for the package to arrive before the stated deadline.

How to Apply for the JET Programme 2027

Applicants should carefully review the official JET Programme information and application documentation before preparing their submissions.

The basic submission process indicated by the Embassy is:

  1. Review the official JET Programme information and application requirements.
  2. Complete the required application documentation.
  3. Prepare the complete application package.
  4. Check that all required documents have been included.
  5. Submit the package by courier with a tracking number or hand deliver it to the Embassy of Japan in Pretoria.
  6. Ensure that the application arrives by 4:00 PM on 16 October 2026.
  7. Wait for notification by email regarding the outcome of the application.

Applicants should ensure that their submissions are complete and comply with the instructions in the official application documentation.

Selection Results

The Embassy of Japan states that both successful and unsuccessful applicants will be contacted by email.

Applicants are specifically requested not to contact the Embassy to enquire about the outcome of their application.

It is therefore important for applicants to monitor the email address provided in their application after submission.

To APPLY download the application form HERE.

Important Considerations Before Applying

The JET Programme can be a major international and professional opportunity, but applicants should understand the commitment involved.

Before applying, prospective participants should consider whether they are prepared to:

  • Live in Japan for at least one year.
  • Adapt to a different cultural and social environment.
  • Work within the Japanese education system.
  • Follow the instructions of their supervisors and Contracting Organisations.
  • Interact professionally with students, teachers and community members.
  • Represent South Africa responsibly.
  • Participate actively in international and cultural exchange.
  • Accept the responsibilities associated with their assigned position.
  • Commit to the programme rather than treating it simply as an opportunity for travel.

The programme is intended for individuals who can make a meaningful contribution while adapting to life and work in Japan.

Visit HERE to learn more about the JET Programme 2027.

Conclusion

The JET Programme 2027 offers young South African university graduates an opportunity to spend at least one year in Japan while working as Assistant Language Teachers and contributing to international exchange.

The programme combines language education, professional experience, community engagement and cultural exchange. Participants can work alongside Japanese teachers and educational authorities, support foreign-language classes, assist with teaching materials and extracurricular activities, contribute to speech contests and participate in local international exchange initiatives.

Beyond the professional responsibilities, the programme provides an opportunity to experience Japanese society from within a local community while helping Japanese students and residents learn more about South Africa and the wider world.

Interested South African graduates should begin preparing their applications well before the deadline. The complete application package must arrive at the Embassy of Japan in Pretoria no later than 4:00 PM on 16 October 2026.

For the official application instructions, detailed information and application forms, applicants should consult the Embassy of Japan in South Africa’s official JET Programme information before submitting their documents.
